cards.title: Do classical one-way functions exist?
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer d≥1, there is n₀ with Pr[f(I(1ⁿ,f(X)))=f(X)]≤n⁻ᵈ for all n≥n₀, where X is uniform on {0,1}ⁿ and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

progress.text: Levin gives a combinatorial complete function, one-way if any one-way function exists.
Liu and Pass characterize one-way-function existence by average-case hardness of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity.
Hirahara and Nanashima characterize the hypothetical Pessiland setting; neither existence nor impossibility of one-way functions follows unconditionally.

cards.definitions: The security parameter n≥1 is given in unary as 1ⁿ. A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains 1ⁿ, so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives f(X), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when f(Y)=f(X); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most n⁻ᵈ for each integer d≥1. The threshold n₀ can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some d≥1 it exceeds n⁻ᵈ for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
context_blocks.text: One-way functions would imply P≠NP, since P=NP would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether P≠NP alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither P≠NP nor any candidate’s hardness.

context_blocks.title: What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.title: Does computationally secure public-key encryption exist?
cards.formal: Do there exist uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc and Dec forming a public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages with negligible correctness error and IND-CPA security against every uniform classical probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, with these properties proved without an unproved hardness assumption?
cards.why: Would establish the existence of secure public communication from a mathematical theorem rather than a computational assumption.

progress.text: Goldreich gives precise encryption security definitions, conditional constructions and relations to one-way functions.
Regev constructs classical public-key encryption under learning-with-errors hardness.
Lu and coauthors obtain classical public-key encryption from assumed average-case hardness of stabilizer decoding.

cards.definitions: For security parameter n≥1, Gen(1ⁿ) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m) takes a bit m∈{0,1} and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over m∈{0,1} of Pr[Dec(1ⁿ,sk,Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary A₁ receives (1ⁿ,pk) and outputs bits m₀,m₁ and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate c=Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m_b), and give (1ⁿ,pk,z,c) to its second stage A₂, which outputs a bit b′. For every pair (A₁,A₂), |Pr[b′=b]−1/2| must be negligible. A function η(n) is negligible if, for every integer d≥1, η(n)≤n⁻ᵈ for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success 1/2. Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence P≠NP. The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
